description: What does it take to build a world from scratch - and what does the act of building one reveal about storytelling, culture, and imagination? Dungeons & Dragons has been inviting players to answer that question for over 50 years, drawing on a rich literary tradition that runs from Tolkien and Jack Vance to contemporary film, television, and live-play streams like Critical Role. In this seminar, we trace the literary DNA of D&D: the foundational texts that shaped the game, the world-building traditions they created, and how those traditions became a global cultural phenomenon. We treat world-building itself as a writing practice - a way of making arguments about how societies work, what we value, and what we fear. Major writing assignments will move from close analysis of texts and games to research-driven argumentation and reflection. Students will also learn practical skills for engaging AI as a thought partner to strengthen their own writing - learning how to use it and when not to use it. Students with reservations about AI will always have non-AI alternatives. No prior experience with D&D is required or expected.
